title: The Divinity Verses Examined One by One
subtitle: John 1:1, 8:58, 10:30, 20:28, Philippians 2:6-8, Colossians 2:9, and Titus 2:13 — the Greek grammar, the Trinitarian case, and the unitarian case, side by side
summary: Several New Testament passages genuinely support belief in Jesus's divinity, while the same record presents his prayer and dependence on God. Christianity reconciles those features through incarnation; Islam finds the human-messenger account better warranted. The case concerns both Jesus's identity and the authority of the texts through which it is known, with the Quran offering a definite prophetic correction.

seo.metaTitle: The Divinity Verses Examined One by One: John 1:1 to Titus 2:13
seo.metaDescription: The strongest New Testament texts for Jesus's divinity, considered honestly alongside his prayer and dependence and Islam's case for worshiping God alone.

sections.title: The Strongest Texts Belong in the Discussion
sections.body:
Some New Testament texts call Jesus God or describe him in language Christians reasonably understand as divine. Islam does not need a strained translation of every one to maintain its conclusion.

The larger issue is authority: why take the Quran's prophetic account as the correction where these texts disagree? Read [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran) alongside this study. Without that wider case, quoting the Quran cannot settle a Christian reader's question.

sections.title: More Than Seven Isolated Proof Texts
sections.body:
John 1:1, 8:58, 10:30, and 20:28, Philippians 2, Colossians 2:9, and Titus 2:13 form part of a cumulative Christian account. Christians read them with Jesus's life, resurrection, and the wider apostolic witness.

A word's possible meaning elsewhere does not decide its meaning here. The question is what each passage contributes in context and whether its authority warrants identifying a worshiping human life with the eternal Creator.

sections.title: Meaning, Context, and Authority
sections.body:
First ask what the wording most naturally means in its context. Then ask how it fits the author's wider portrait of Jesus, including his prayers and dependence on God. Finally ask whether that text has the authority to determine belief about God.

Christians treat the New Testament's witness as revelation. Islam does not accept every claim by every biblical author on that basis. Distinguishing a narrator's words from Jesus's words is useful, but does not by itself disprove the narrator.

sections.title: John 1:1: A Strong Prologue, Not a Translation Trick
sections.body:
John's prologue says the Word was with God and was God, and later says the Word became flesh. It gives Christians substantial grounds for incarnation. Rendering the phrase simply 'a god' is not a sound shortcut to an Islamic conclusion.

Muslims can consider biblical language of God's word and wisdom while acknowledging that John's prologue goes beyond merely calling Jesus a good prophet. Islam's rejection of incarnation rests on its account of God and revelation, not on pretending the prologue clearly teaches the Quran's view.

sections.title: John 8:58: Do Not Ignore the Reference to Abraham
sections.body:
The saying places Jesus before Abraham. The words 'I am' also occur in ordinary speech, but that fact does not remove their force in this exchange. Christians read preexistence and, in the wider Johannine setting, divine identity.

Muslim readings that take precedence as God's prior plan are interpretations, not an uncontested meaning supplied by the Greek words alone. The verse must be weighed with Jesus's distinction between himself and the God who sent him.

sections.title: John 10:30: Unity, Authority, and Being Sent
sections.body:
Jesus joins his protection of followers to the Father's and says they are one. Christians read more than shared purpose here, especially with the following blasphemy charge and the language of mutual indwelling. Muslims note that John 17:21-22 also uses unity language for disciples, so the word 'one' alone cannot prove shared deity.

Jesus's appeal to Psalm 82:6 must also be read carefully. Interpreters differ about its 'gods'; Christians commonly read a lesser-to-greater defense, while Muslims emphasize Jesus's consecration and mission. Neither the opponents' accusation nor an isolated word settles the whole passage.

sections.title: John 20:28: Thomas Addresses Jesus as God
sections.body:
The text says Thomas speaks to Jesus and calls him Lord and God. It is one of the clearest Christian passages and should not be reduced to an exclamation addressed elsewhere. [Read the chapter itself](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/john/20).

John 20:17 also has Jesus speak of his God. Christians reconcile those statements through incarnation. Muslims regard Jesus's worship and dependence as the clearer guide and do not accept Thomas's confession in John's narrative as overriding the Quran. That is a judgment about revelation, not a denial of what the verse says.

sections.title: Philippians 2: Read Through the Exaltation
sections.body:
Philippians 2:5-11 describes Christ in the form of God, self-humbling, obedience to death, exaltation by God, and universal homage. Many read a preexistent Christ; other readings stress a contrast with Adam. The [whole passage](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/philippians/2) is more substantial than a simple statement that Jesus was obedient.

Islam honors his obedience but rejects the account of incarnation and saving death. The high language is already in this early Christian text, not something that first appeared at fourth-century councils. Its meaning and authority, rather than a false late-invention story, are the actual points of disagreement.

sections.title: Colossians 2:9: Fullness of Deity Is Strong Language
sections.body:
Colossians describes the fullness of deity dwelling bodily in Christ. Christians reasonably take this as evidence for incarnation. Ephesians 3:19's prayer that believers be filled with God's fullness is a useful comparison, but the wording and contexts are not identical; it does not make Colossians an obvious reference only to spiritual gifts.

Islam recognizes the claim's force and asks whether this Christian account is true revelation. It does not adopt a text's authority merely because it preserves other truths about Jesus.

sections.title: Titus 2:13: A Divine Title Cannot Be Dismissed
sections.body:
Many translations read this as calling Jesus our great God and Savior. Another reading distinguishes God from Jesus; the [USCCB note](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/titus/2) records the alternative translation. The wording is significant evidence for divine language about Christ.

Debate about Titus's authorship matters historically, but disputed authorship alone does not prove a statement false. Islam's case remains the distinction between God's authority and the authority Christians assign to this letter.

sections.title: The Quran's Clear Account of Jesus
sections.body:
The Quran defines Jesus as Messiah, word conveyed to Mary, spirit from Him, and messenger, while rejecting divine sonship (4:171). His miraculous creation is compared with Adam's (3:59). He calls people to worship his Lord and theirs (5:72), identifies himself as God's servant and prophet (19:30), and is described with Mary as eating food (5:75).

Together these give Muslims a consistent account of created dependence and extraordinary God-given honor. They supply Islam's revealed framework, not a proof that can assume the Quran's authority before a seeker has examined it.

sections.title: Dependence, Two Natures, and the Remaining Question
sections.body:
John 17:3 names the Father as the only true God and Jesus as the one sent. John 14:28 says the Father is greater, and Mark 13:32 describes the Son not knowing the Hour. These are positive evidence of a real relationship of dependence.

The Christian two-natures reply is that the one Son possesses both divine and human natures: his human mind, will, prayer, and obedience are genuinely finite without making his divine nature limited. This is not a claim that an abstract nature prays by itself; the person lives a human life. The [Catholic Catechism, paragraphs 469-475](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P1J.HTM), develops that account, including human knowledge and will.

Islam's reply is that this distinction can reconcile the statements within Christian theology, but belief that the union occurred requires positive evidence. Dependence, being sent, and worship are fully explained by a human messenger. Identifying that life with an uncreated divine person requires additional positive evidence, and the passages above supply the Christian case for it. Muslims find that case insufficient to cross the Creator-messenger boundary and accept the Quran's consistent account of Jesus as servant and prophet. The conclusion is comparative, not the claim that one prayer logically disproves every two-natures explanation.

sections.title: Not Every High Title Means the Same Thing
sections.body:
Elevated language can express granted authority, while some New Testament passages go further. Treating every divine title as an ordinary honorific does not fit the strength of texts such as John 20:28.

Islam accepts Jesus's extraordinary honor without receiving every Christian interpretation as revelation. The Quran's claim to correct earlier disagreement needs reasons of its own. Its positive account joins one self-sufficient Creator with human messengers who direct worship to Him, rather than promising that every surviving Christian text already teaches Islamic doctrine.

sections.title: Choose Worship on the Strength of the Whole Case
sections.body:
The Muslim conclusion is that Jesus's human dependence and God's incomparable self-sufficiency belong on opposite sides of the Creator-creature distinction. The Quran confirms that distinction while honoring Jesus's extraordinary rank.

Read [Incarnation Explained](/articles/incarnation-explained) for Christianity's strongest way of joining the two, then [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran) for the authority behind Islam's correction. Seek truth with reverence; neither love of Jesus nor honest examination needs to be surrendered.

sections.title: Focused Questions
sections.body:
Q: Which of the seven passages has the strongest grammatical case for calling Jesus God outright?
A: John 20:28 directly has Thomas address Jesus as God. Titus 2:13 is also commonly translated as applying God and Savior to Jesus, though another reading separates the referents. It is unnecessary to rank their grammar as though one verse alone resolves the entire theology.

Q: Is Colwell’s rule a reliable proof that John 1:1 calls Jesus “God” rather than “a god”?
A: No single grammatical rule proves the whole doctrine. John 1:1 must be read with the Word being with God and the Word becoming flesh. The prologue is strong Christian evidence, not a clear statement of the Islamic position.

Q: Is the “I AM” of John 8:58 definitely a claim to be the God of Exodus 3:14?
A: The reference to Abraham makes this a serious claim of precedence, often understood as preexistence. Ordinary uses of 'I am' elsewhere do not settle its force here. Its relation to divine identity must be assessed in John's wider account.

Q: Does the Bible ever call Jesus God directly, in so many words?
A: Yes, several texts naturally support that reading, especially John 20:28. Islam does not need to deny this. It examines those texts alongside Jesus's dependence and accepts the Quran as the correction where the accounts disagree.

Q: Is the exclamation reading of John 20:28 as strong as the qualitative reading of John 1:1?
A: No. Thomas addresses Jesus in the text; redirecting the words as an exclamation to someone else does not fit that wording. The disagreement concerns the truth and authority of the confession within the larger account, not whether Thomas says it.

Q: Does presenting both readings mean the question of Jesus’s divinity can’t be answered?
A: No. It makes the real question clear: which account of God, Jesus, and revelation is best warranted? Islam offers a definite conclusion—honor Jesus as Messiah and worship the Creator alone—while requiring its own claim to revelation to be examined.

furtherReading.title: Jesus as God: The New Testament Use of Theos in Reference to Jesus
furtherReading.author: Murray J. Harris
furtherReading.note: The standard technical, mainstream defense of reading theos as applied to Jesus in the New Testament, with detailed treatments of John 1:1, John 20:28, and Titus 2:13.

furtherReading.title: The Climax of the Covenant: Christ and the Law in Pauline Theology
furtherReading.author: N. T. Wright
furtherReading.note: Collects Wright's influential 1986 essay on harpagmos and Philippians 2:5-11, the strongest modern statement of the kenotic, pre-existence reading.

furtherReading.title: Christology in the Making: A New Testament Inquiry into the Origins of the Doctrine of the Incarnation
furtherReading.author: James D. G. Dunn
furtherReading.note: Presents the Adam-Christology reading of Philippians 2 and argues that New Testament belief in Jesus's pre-existence developed within, rather than from the start of, the earliest tradition.

furtherReading.title: The Doctrine of the Trinity: Christianity's Self-Inflicted Wound
furtherReading.author: Anthony F. Buzzard and Charles F. Hunting
furtherReading.note: The fullest modern statement of the Christian unitarian case against the seven passages examined here , offered so readers can weigh its arguments directly.
